title: Pueblo County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Pueblo County wells have a 46-foot median depth. Compare yields, water levels, drilling records and estimated finished-well costs of $7,600-$14,500.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Pueblo County
intro_html:
A shallow countywide median does not guarantee a shallow well on your lot. Pueblo County’s recorded median depth is 46 feet, but the middle half runs from 32 to 184 feet, and deeper drilling is a real possibility.

Colorado DWR records contain 12,231 permitted wells across the county, with 7,958 recorded as constructed. Use those records to narrow your search around Pueblo West, Avondale, Rye or the area where you plan to buy—not as a substitute for checking the actual property.

sections.heading: A 46-Foot Median Hides Pueblo County’s Deeper Wells
sections.html:
Among the 8,251 wells reporting depth, 68% are under 100 feet. The median is 46 feet, but the middle half spans 32–184 feet. For a drilling bid, that means the county median is a starting point, not a dependable footage allowance. The 90th-percentile depth is 520 feet.

Ground conditions include alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permit entries name Dakota for 275 wells and Alluvial for 171; another 11,416 fall in an unnamed / fractured-bedrock category. That broad category does not establish the formation beneath your parcel. Compare nearby completion logs around Vineland or Boone separately from those around Beulah Valley, and ask the driller which water-bearing formation the bid targets.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Usually Clear the Low-Output Range
sections.html:
The 1,657 wells with reported pump yields have a 10.7 gpm median, with the middle half producing 7.5–15.0 gpm. That range can support ordinary household demand when the well sustains its output and the pump and pressure system are properly sized. A recorded drilling-time yield is not a current performance guarantee.

Only 1% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, while 8% fall in the 1–5 gpm group. Those lower-output wells deserve careful attention to recovery, storage and peak household demand. Before buying, get a current pumping evaluation rather than relying on the county median. Also check permitted uses: available flow does not automatically authorize irrigation or livestock watering.

sections.heading: Recent Water-Level Records Are Deeper, but Not a Parcel Forecast
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the drilled depth or the water level while pumping. Pueblo County has 577 records reporting it, with a median of 50 feet below ground and a middle half of 21–191 feet. These are a different reporting group from the depth records, so the medians should not be treated as measurements of the same well.

Decade medians move from 25 feet in the 1960s to 20 in the 1980s, then 33 in the 2010s and 99 in the 2020s. Recent measurements are substantially deeper, but this is not a steady decline through the whole series. Different locations and aquifers may explain part of the change; repeated measurements from nearby comparable wells are more useful.

sections.heading: Permit Activity Runs Through 2025
sections.html:
Pueblo County’s permit history includes 1,893 permits issued in the 1990s and 2,389 in the 2000s, followed by 1,358 in the 2010s. The records show 699 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, so its total is not directly comparable with a finished decade.

Frequently listed driller names include Don Stewart & Son Drilling (Stewart, Donald D), with 501 records, and Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.), with 490. The larger entry, “Authorized (Pe, Pg),” has 1,486 records but should not be treated as a confirmed drilling-company name. Historical record counts show past activity, not present availability or a recommendation.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole in Pueblo County
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $35–$55 per foot for drilling through alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 46-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $1,600–$2,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,600–$14,500.

Those figures describe the median-depth case, not a countywide fixed-price package. The 32–184-foot middle range alone leaves substantial room for footage differences. Ask for a written scope covering casing, grout, well development, pump selection and connections to the house. Have the contractor explain extra-depth charges and what happens financially if the initial hole does not produce usable water. Access and the final site layout also belong in the discussion.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Septic Before Closing
sections.html:
The environmental screening inventory lists 56 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 34 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites and 5 historic mine features within about 10 miles. These mapped sites are reasons to investigate the parcel’s surroundings, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A sampling location is not automatically a confirmed contamination source.

Use laboratory testing to establish drinking-water quality, and ask whether nearby site histories warrant targeted testing. Inspect the wellhead, casing condition and drainage around it. Low reported yields also warrant a current performance check; a neighboring successful well cannot guarantee a productive new hole. For building, confirm that the well, septic system, replacement septic area and house can fit with the required separations before committing to a layout.

sections.heading: Make the Lot Decision With Local Logs and the Actual Permit
sections.html:
Start close to the property. A countywide search is useful background, but a buyer in Blende or Salt Creek should first examine surrounding completion records rather than borrowing expectations from Colorado City or Rye. Look for matching geology, drilled depths, reported yields and recent water-level measurements.

Then read the actual DWR permit. Domestic/household use appears on 54% of county records, but that does not establish what your permit allows. Confirm household, outdoor and stock uses individually. In an over-appropriated basin, a proposed use may require an augmentation plan unless it qualifies for an exemption. Make purchase or construction commitments contingent on permit suitability, well performance, water quality and a workable site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Pueblo County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 46 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 184 feet. Although 68% are under 100 feet, the 90th-percentile depth is 520 feet. Check completion logs near the parcel and in comparable geology before using the county median to set your drilling budget.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Pueblo County?
faq.a: The drilling model is $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 46-foot median depth, the hole alone is about $1,600–$2,500, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,600–$14,500. A deeper target or different installation scope can change the quote, so get itemized pricing for the actual lot.

faq.q: How much water do Pueblo County wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 10.7 gpm, with the middle half at 7.5–15.0 gpm. Among reporting wells, 1% yield under 1 gpm and 8% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Have an existing well evaluated for sustained output and recovery; its historical yield may not describe current performance.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Pueblo County?
faq.a: County permit records cannot establish drinking-water safety for an individual home. The mapped screening inventory includes 56 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 34 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but proximity alone does not prove a well is affected. Obtain laboratory testing and review nearby environmental records before relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Pueblo County?
faq.a: Reported decade medians show deeper recent water levels: 33 feet below ground in the 2010s and 99 feet in the 2020s. Earlier decades fluctuate, so the series does not establish a uniform countywide decline. Compare repeated measurements from nearby wells in the same aquifer before drawing conclusions about a property’s long-term supply.
